title: Starting vox
summary: What happens between typing `vox notes.txt` and seeing the file on screen.

steps.text: The program starts here. `cli::parse` reads the arguments: the file to open and the mode (`--local-config [DIR]`, `--vanilla`, or global by default).
Turns the arguments into a mode and a file. `--local-config` takes a following argument as the project folder only if it is a directory, so `vox --local-config notes.txt` still opens the file.
Reads the file into a String with the standard library. A missing file is fine: you get an empty document that will be created on `:w`.
Detects the line ending (`\n` or `\r\n`) and removes the final newline. It is remembered and written back on save, so every stored line is a visible line.
The storage factory. The document does not know which storage it uses; the binary passes this function in. Here it creates the fast tree-based storage from the `vox-storage` adapter.

Creates the editor. `Services` carries the three platform pieces: text storage factory, char width rules (`vox-width`), and the system clipboard (`vox-clipboard`). It also registers the built-in commands.
Registers `:write`, `:quit`, `:edit`, `:wq`, `:xit` and their short names (`w`, `q`, `e`, `x`) in the command registry: the same API a plugin uses.
Reads the active scope's `config.toml` (global `~/.config/vox/`, or the project's `.vox/` with `--local-config`; nothing with `--vanilla`) and applies it.
Loads every `*.wasm` file from the active scope's plugin folder. A broken plugin only produces a notification.
Sends the first `BufOpen` event, so plugins learn which file is open.
The main loop. It repeats: measure the terminal, draw the editor, wait for a key, give the key to the editor. It stops when the editor says it should quit.
Puts the terminal in raw mode (keys arrive one by one, nothing is echoed) and switches to the alternate screen. A panic hook restores the terminal if anything crashes.
Tells the editor the terminal size so it can keep the cursor visible.
Builds a `Surface`: a grid of cells describing the whole screen. Pure: it only reads editor state.
Sends the surface to the real terminal, rewriting only the rows that changed since the last frame.
Waits for the next key press.
Converts the terminal library's key event into vox's own `Key` type, so the editor never sees third-party types.

The single entry point for input. It first checks the key against the user's mappings, then sends it to the handler for the current mode, then scrolls so the cursor stays visible. The loop then draws again.

title: Starting a project with --local-config
summary: `vox --local-config notes.txt` in a project that has no `.vox/` yet, then choosing “Copy everything”.

steps.text: Mode: local, no folder given.
Looks upward from the current folder for a `.vox/`. None found, so the current folder is the project.
The active scope: config, plugins, and lockfile all live in `<project>/.vox/`.
The editor learns the active scope (for `:scope` and the `LOCAL` badge) and the global one (the source for copying).
Tries the project's `config.toml`: it does not exist yet, so nothing is applied. `:reload config` is registered for the project path anyway.
Same for plugins: the project's plugin folder is empty for now. The global plugins are not loaded.
Because `.vox/` does not exist, `main` runs `:scope setup`: a dialog listing what can be copied from the global setup.
“Copy everything” runs `:scope init all`.
Creates `.vox/plugins/` and copies `config.toml` and each global plugin, never overwriting existing files.
Runs `:reload config` and `:reload plugins`, which read from the project paths: the copied config and plugins are active immediately.

title: Pressing d then w (delete a word)
summary: How two key presses become one Vim command that edits the text.

steps.text: Key `d` arrives. It is added to the mapping buffer.
No user mapping starts with `d`, so the key goes straight to `dispatch`, which sends it to `handle_normal` because the mode is Normal.
Adds `d` to the list of pending keys and asks the parser whether the keys form a complete command.
`d` alone is an operator waiting for a motion, so the answer is Incomplete. Nothing happens yet; the editor waits. Then `w` arrives and `dw` parses to: operator Delete, target = motion WordForward.
Runs the parsed command. An operator command goes to `operate`.
Finds out which text the operator covers. For a motion target it asks where the motion lands, then builds a range from the cursor to that point.
For `w` with an operator it uses `next_word_start`. Vim rule: if the next word is on another line, `dw` stops at the end of the current line instead.
Pure function in core: walks chars from the cursor, skipping the current word and then whitespace. Empty lines count as words.
Copies the text in the range into a register (so `p` can paste it back), then deletes it.
Stores the deleted text in the unnamed register (or the system clipboard for `"+`).
Removes the text from storage and records the change in the undo history.
The storage trait. In the real editor this is `vox-storage`'s implementation; in tests it is `SimpleStorage`. The document only knows the trait.
Remembers the removed text and where it was, so undo can put it back.
Closes the recorded edits into one undo step: one `u` will undo the whole `dw`.
Puts the cursor at the start of the deleted range, clamped to a valid column.
Back in `handle_key`: scrolls the view if the cursor left the screen. The next loop iteration draws the result.
`i` parses to the action Insert(Before).
Runs the insert action.
Switches to Insert mode. The cursor may now sit after the last char of a line.
Each typed char is inserted at the cursor. `Enter` inserts a line ending, `Backspace` deletes (joining lines at column 0).
Inserts text into storage, records it in history (not yet committed), and returns the position after the new text.
Storage trait call; the real implementation lives in `vox-storage`.
`Esc`: commits all edits of this insert session as one undo step, switches back to Normal mode, and moves the cursor one left (like Vim).
`:` parses to the action CommandLine.
Switches to Command mode with an empty input line.
Typed chars are appended to the input. `Enter` takes the input and runs it as a command line.
Looks the command up in the registry and calls it. An `Err` from the command becomes the message (e.g. `E37: No write since last change`).
Splits `w! notes.txt` into the name `w`, the force flag `!`, and the argument `notes.txt`.
Finds the command by name or alias: `w` is an alias of `write`.
The built-in `write` command. It is an ordinary registered command; a plugin could replace it.
Checks there is a file name, saves, and shows a message like `"notes.txt" 3L, 42B written`.
Writes the text plus the remembered final newline with the standard library, then marks the current undo step as the saved state.
Now false: the current undo step equals the saved one. The status line drops `[+]`. Undoing past the save makes it true again.

title: A key mapping: jk leaves insert mode
summary: With `jk = "<Esc>"` under `[keymap.insert]` in the config, typing `j` then `k`.

steps.text: `j` arrives and is added to the mapping buffer.
Asks the keymap whether the buffered keys match a mapping for Insert mode.
`j` is the start of `jk` but not a full mapping: the answer is Prefix. Nothing is inserted yet.
Now true. The run loop sees this and waits only `timeout_ms` (default 1000 ms) for the next key.
If no key comes in time, the loop calls `Editor::timeout`, and `j` is inserted as typed. Here `k` arrives in time.
`jk` matches exactly: the binding is the keys `<Esc>`.
Feeds `<Esc>` to the mode handler. Mapped keys are not mapped again (like Vim's `noremap`). A binding written as `":w"` would run a command instead.
Sends the key to the handler for the current mode, here `handle_insert`, which leaves Insert mode.
The other path: when the wait ends, a full match is used (e.g. a mapping for `g` when `gx` also exists), otherwise the keys are handled as typed.

title: Loading the config file
summary: How `~/.config/vox/config.toml` becomes key mappings, with the file format kept out of core.

steps.text: Called once at start-up by `main` with the active scope's config path (none in vanilla mode).
Adapter: the global folder: `$VOX_CONFIG_DIR`, else `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/vox`, else `~/.config/vox`. The binary turns it into the global scope; in local or vanilla mode a different scope is used.
Adapter: reads the file. A missing file is not an error: vox runs with defaults.
Adapter: parses TOML with the `toml` library. Syntax errors keep their line number.
Adapter: converts the library's values to vox's own `Value` tree, so core never sees a `toml` type.
Core: checks every setting. Unknown settings and wrong types are collected as errors, but the valid parts are still used.
Core: sets the mapping timeout and turns each mapping into keys and a binding.
Replaces `<leader>` with the leader key and parses Vim key notation (`<C-s>`, `<Esc>`).
A right side starting with `:` runs a command; anything else is keys. An empty string disables the key.
Stores the mapping, replacing an earlier one for the same keys.

title: Drawing one frame
summary: How editor state becomes characters in the terminal.

steps.text: Creates an empty surface the size of the terminal and fills it in parts.
For each visible row: line number (dim), then the visible part of the line; `~` past the end of the file.
Cuts the part of a line that fits on screen, after horizontal scrolling. Tabs become spaces; wide chars cut at an edge become spaces.
How many cells a char takes. A trait: the real editor uses `vox-width` (Unicode rules: 2 for CJK), tests use `Monospace` (always 1).
Writes text into the cell grid with a style, clipping at the right edge.
In visual mode, marks the selected cells as reversed.
The reversed status line: mode, file name, `[+]`, cursor position.
The bottom line: the `:` or `/` prompt being typed, or the last message.
Open panels and the modal are drawn as bordered boxes on top, with their views inside.
Notifications are drawn last, so they are always visible.
Where the terminal cursor goes: in the `:` prompt, in a focused view (or hidden if the view has none), or in the text, converting the cursor's char column to screen cells.
Compares each row with the previous frame and prints only changed rows, then places the cursor and sets its shape (block or bar).

title: Opening a panel: :keymaps
summary: How a command fills the side panel, and how keys reach it.

steps.text: The `:keymaps` command builds one list row per user mapping, e.g. `n <Space>w → :w`.
Puts the list view in the side panel and moves focus there.
From now on the layout has a side panel: the text area gets narrower, and scrolling uses the new width.
Pure function: splits the screen into text, side panel, bottom panel, modal, and notification areas using the `[ui]` settings.
The next key: no modal is open, and the side panel has focus...
...so `<C-w>` and `:` keep working, and every other key goes to the panel's view.
Gives the key to the view and acts on its answer: close it, run a command line, or nothing.
`j`/`k` move the selection; `Enter` returns the row's command; `q` returns Close.
When drawing, the panel gets a border with its title, highlighted while focused, and the view draws inside it.

title: A notification's life
summary: `:notify error disk full`: shown, kept in history, gone after 4 seconds without any key press.

steps.text: Reads the optional level (`info`, `warn`, `error`) and the text.
Stores the notification with an expiry time (now + `notify_timeout_ms`, from the injected clock) and adds it to the history.
Draws each notification as a colored box in the configured corner, wrapped to at most 3 lines.
Tells the run loop the earliest time something must happen: here, the expiry.
Waits for a key, but only until that deadline, then calls `tick` and draws again.
Removes expired notifications (and times out pending key mappings). The next frame no longer shows the box.
`u` parses to the action Undo (with an optional count, e.g. `3u`).
Asks the document to undo one step; shows a message if there is nothing to undo.
Takes the last undo group and reverses its edits in reverse order (remove what was inserted, insert what was removed). The group moves to the redo stack.
Storage calls that actually change the text.
Moves the cursor to where the change happened.
`/` parses to the action Search; the editor switches to the search prompt.
Collects `foo`; `Enter` runs the search.
Remembers `foo` as the last pattern (an empty pattern repeats the previous one) and jumps.
Repeats the search `count` times and sets the message (wrap notice or `E486: Pattern not found`).
Pure function in core: literal text search after (or before) the cursor, wrapping around the end of the file.
Later, `n` parses to the motion SearchNext, which uses the same `search_target`. Because it is a motion, `dn` (delete to next match) also works.

title: Copying to the system clipboard with "+yy
summary: How a register prefix reaches the operating system's clipboard.

steps.text: `"+` sets the register to `+`; `yy` is operator Yank on whole lines.
Builds a linewise range for the current line.
Copies the line text and stores it in register `+`. Yank does not change the text.
Register `+` (or `*`) means the system clipboard; anything else is the unnamed register.
The clipboard trait defined in core. Core never talks to the OS directly.
The adapter implementation, using the `arboard` library (X11, Wayland, macOS, Windows).

title: Adding your own command (developer API)
summary: How code registers a new `:` command, and how it runs.

steps.text: Gives access to the command registry, e.g. `ed.commands_mut()`.
`register("upper", "description", |ed, args| { ... Ok(()) })`. Registering an existing name replaces it, so built-ins can be overridden.
Optional short name: `alias("up", "upper")`.
Runs it from `:up! arg`, from a key mapping like `"<leader>u" = ":upper"`, or directly from code. The handler gets `Args { arg, force }` and may return `Err(message)`.

title: Loading a plugin
summary: How the package `text-tools/` (with `plugin.toml`) in the plugin folder is checked, loaded, and given its settings.

steps.text: Creates the plugin host with the TOML parser from `vox-config-file` and loads the active scope's plugin folder.
Finds all plugins in the folder and decides, together, which may load.
Core: every folder and `.wasm` file is a package. A folder must contain `plugin.toml` and `plugin.wasm`.
Reads and validates `plugin.toml` (through the injected parser, so core never parses TOML) and checks the folder name matches.
Turns the manifest into name, version, API version, requirements, and typed settings, collecting every problem.
Applies `enabled = false`, resolves settings against `[plugins.NAME]`, and runs the requirement checks — repeatedly, so a plugin that needs a failed plugin fails too.
API version, vox version, other plugins, programs on PATH. Each unmet requirement gets its level: error (not loaded), warning, info.
For each plugin that may load: start it, call its own `health()`, record the result, and log it.
Compiles the WebAssembly, gives it its own memory-limited store with its effective settings, and calls `init`.
Every call into a plugin goes through here: owner `plugin:NAME`, time budget (about 1 s), and the plugin is stopped if it crashes or breaks a limit.
During `init` the plugin calls `register-command("wordcount", ...)`; the request is queued...
...and installed after the call: a normal editor command whose handler calls back into the plugin.
The plugin's own health findings join the others. An `Error` unloads the plugin again (everything it registered is removed).

title: Running a plugin command
summary: Typing `:upper` with the text-tools plugin loaded.

steps.text: `:upper` is looked up in the registry like any command. The handler was created by the plugin host.
Lends the editor to the plugin and calls its exported `run-command("upper", none, false)` inside the time limit.
The plugin asks for the cursor line's text. Every request from the plugin arrives as a call like this one.
The plugin deletes the old line text...
...and inserts the uppercase text. These go to the same `Editor` functions any code uses.
Core edit API: the change is recorded in the undo history.
Back in core: all edits of the command become one undo step, the cursor is kept valid, and a `TextChanged` event is sent to subscribers.
Plugins that subscribed (for example to `buf-write`) get events through handlers registered here.

title: Reloading a plugin
summary: `:reload plugins text_tools` after rebuilding the plugin.

steps.text: At start-up the binary registered `:reload plugins`; its handler holds the plugin host.
Finds the file the plugin was loaded from.
Removes everything owned by `plugin:text_tools`: its commands, mappings, and event handlers. Their closures held the only references to the old plugin instance, so it is dropped.
If the plugin had replaced a command (say `:xit`), the older registration (the built-in) becomes active again.
Loads the file again (a fresh instance, so a disabled plugin works again) and logs the result with source `plugin:text_tools`.
The plugin's `init` runs under the owner `plugin:text_tools`, so everything it registers can be removed again next time.
Sets the owner for commands, mappings, and subscriptions for the duration of the call.
The config turns developer mode on.
Registers the `:log` commands and three mappings owned by `devmode` (`<leader>dl`, `<leader>dr`, `<leader>dc`) and logs the change. Turning it off removes exactly those and closes open log views.
`<leader>dl` runs `:log`: a `LogView` filled from the log opens in the bottom panel.
Any later log line (a command run, a plugin's `log(...)`) is added to the ring buffer...
...and every open log view is refreshed, so the panel updates live.
In the panel, `f` and `s` change the level and source filters and ask the editor to refresh; `c` clears.
`[plugins.NAME]` tables are kept as they are; only `enabled` is checked here, because the allowed settings are known only from each plugin's manifest.
The host asks the editor for a plugin's user values when it loads the plugin.
Defaults from `[settings.KEY]`, replaced by valid user values. A wrong value (say `case = "shout"`) is ignored with a warning.
Checks one value: type, min/max, or allowed choices.
When the plugin calls `setting("case")`, the host answers from the settings it was given at load time.
`:checkhealth` runs each running plugin's `health()` again...
...and shows every plugin: version, status, each finding (✓ ok, ! warning, ✗ error, i info), and the settings in use.
Opens a list: vox settings, key mappings, and one row per plugin with settings. The title says which file changes go to.
Builds a form from the schema of vox's settings and the current values of the applied config.
One list of typed settings (same type plugins use in `plugin.toml`), with limits matching the config checks. A test keeps it in sync with `Config`.
`Enter` edits the number; the typed value is checked against the limits before it is accepted. `s` returns the changed fields as `Submit`.
`Submit` goes back to the settings list (the form's parent) and runs `:settings save vox` with the submitted values.
Turns each changed field into an edit with a path, e.g. set `ui.side_width` = 32.
Applies the edits to the current config in memory and validates the result first; only then writes the file and applies the new config.
Adapter: edits `config.toml` with `toml_edit`: only the changed keys, comments and layout kept, written to a temp file and renamed.
The new value takes effect immediately (the side panel is narrower on the next frame). For plugin settings, the plugin is reloaded too.
Reads the source: a git URL with `@v0.1.0`. Takes the active scope's paths (plugin folder, lockfile, `.build/` work folder) and starts a background job, so vox stays usable while it builds.
Git URL or folder? `@REF` is only taken after the last `/`, so `git@host:...` stays intact.
Runs the work on a thread. Progress lines (cloning, building, installing) arrive as notifications.
Clones the repository, checks out the tag, and records the exact commit (`git rev-parse HEAD`).
Reads `plugin.toml`; a project is built with cargo for `wasm32-wasip2`. The package is assembled in a temp folder and renamed into place.
`cargo build --release --target wasm32-wasip2` into the scope's `.build/` folder; the output name comes from `Cargo.toml`.
SHA-256 of the installed `plugin.wasm`, computed with std only.
Back on the editor's thread: the job's result arrives through a channel.
Adds the entry to `vox.lock` (name, version, url, ref, rev, checksum).
Runs `:reload plugins hello`, which loads the new plugin with health checks as usual.

title: Setting up a cloned project: :plugins sync
summary: A fresh clone has `.vox/config.toml` and `.vox/vox.lock` but no installed plugins.

steps.text: At start-up vox compares the installed plugins with the lockfile and says that plugins are missing.
Per plugin: ok (same checksum), missing, changed, or installed but not locked.
`:plugins sync` takes the missing and changed ones and installs them in a background job.
Installs exactly what the lock says: git at the recorded commit, or the recorded path.
The lockfile is read through the injected TOML parser; core never parses TOML itself.

title: Turning a plugin off in the plugin manager

steps.text: `<leader>p` is a default mapping to `:plugins`, made again whenever the leader changes.
Opens the manager as a modal or in the side panel, per `[ui] plugin_manager`.
Builds the rows from the plugin host's infos (`Editor::plugin_infos`), the commands and keys each plugin owns, and `vox.lock` (sources, missing plugins).
`Space` returns `Outcome::Run("plugin disable NAME")`: every action is a command.
Saves `[plugins.NAME] enabled = false` with the M9 config writer (comments kept) and reloads the plugin, which the host now skips as disabled.
After the key is handled, open views refresh, so the row now reads `disabled`.
`:?plugin add` is rewritten to `:help plugin add` before the command is looked up.
Finds what the topic names: a command or alias (`w` → `write`), or a group of subcommands (`plugin`).
The help comes from metadata added when the command was registered: `.category()`, `.param()`, `.force()`, `.returns()`, `.example()`.
Builds the page: breadcrumb path, description, usage (`Command::usage`), parameters, examples, subcommands.
`Enter` on a subcommand returns `Outcome::RunAndClose("help NAME")`; the editor keeps this dialog in the modal history, so `Esc` comes back. `r` returns `commands run NAME`.
Runs the command at once, or opens an `Input` for its arguments when a parameter is required.

title: Finding a command in the browser

steps.text: `:commands` builds the tree and opens it in the modal or the side panel, per `[ui] commands`.
Groups commands by category, then by root word; a root that is also a command lists itself first among its subcommands.
`/` filters every level: entries whose path matches come first, then entries whose description does. `Enter` jumps there.
`l` goes in, `h` goes back; `Enter` on a command returns `commands run NAME`, `?` returns `help NAME` — as `RunAndClose` in the modal so `Esc` comes back, as `Run` in a panel so it stays open.
Shows as many columns as fit (parent, current, preview of the selection's children), the breadcrumb, and the selection's description and usage.
`:` starts the prompt and resets the menu and history position (the typed text lives in `Mode::Command`).
With `completion = "auto"`, every render asks for completions of the line typed so far.
Splits the line into words: the first is a command or alias, the second may name a subcommand, then the parameter at that position says where values come from (`Complete`).
`Tab` takes the only match, the common part, or starts cycling; arrows move in the menu or, without one, walk the history; `Enter` remembers the line and runs it.
Draws the prompt where `[ui] cmdline` says (bottom line, float, or modal) with the menu and the usage title, the current parameter highlighted.
`:e FILE` no longer replaces the document: it opens a buffer (only `:e` alone reloads the current file).
Shows an already open file, or loads it, parks the current document with its cursor and view, and gives the new one the next number (an empty start buffer is replaced).
`:bp` swaps the parked buffer back into `doc` / `cursor` / `view`, so the rest of the editor only ever sees one document.
`:q` looks at every buffer: E37 for this one, E162 naming another with unsaved changes.
`<leader>f` is a default mapping to `:narrow out`.
Without focus it takes the innermost unit at the cursor; with focus, the next larger unit around it.
Asks the `Structure` in use for the units around the cursor line, innermost first.
Matches braces (skipping strings and comments), finds `:`-indented blocks, and names each range from its first line: function, class, or block.
After each edit the focused range moves or grows with the lines added or removed.
Lines outside the focus are drawn dimmed; the status line shows `FOCUS function NAME (Lx–y)`.

title: Asking the AI and accepting its change

steps.text: Entering agent mode registers `:ai` and its keys (`<leader>a`, `ga`, `gx`, `]c` …) with owner `agent`, so text mode removes them again.
`:ai` without an instruction opens the Ask AI dialog, naming the target (selection, focused unit, or line).
Builds the request (instruction, whole text, target lines, `ai_model`, `ai_effort`) and runs the `Assistant` in a background job.
The binary's backend runs Claude Code headless (`claude -p`) on the user's Claude login: no API key.
JSON output with a `{"text"}` schema, no tools, no saved session, the configured model and effort.
On stdin: the whole file, then the range and the instruction.
CLI errors (not logged in, usage limits) and refusals become messages; otherwise `structured_output.text` is the new text for the range.
Back on the editor's thread: if the text is unchanged, the answer is diffed against the target lines into hunks — a proposal to review, or applied at once with `ai_apply = "direct"`.
Line LCS; each run of differences becomes one hunk (lines removed, lines added).
Rendering puts each hunk's removed lines (`-`, red) and added lines (`+`, green) in place.
`ga` replaces the hunk's lines as one undo step and moves the later hunks; when none are left the proposal is gone.
